overview.text: Nikita Khrushchev emerged as the Soviet Union's leader after Joseph Stalin's death in 1953. At a closed Communist Party meeting in 1956, his “Secret Speech” condemned Stalin's purges and cult of personality, beginning a limited process of de-Stalinization. Khrushchev also promoted “peaceful coexistence” with capitalist countries, although Cold War rivalry continued. In 1962 he agreed with Fidel Castro to place Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba, triggering a confrontation with the United States known as the Cuban Missile Crisis. The missiles were withdrawn after negotiations. His years in power mixed changes inside the Soviet system with grave international tension, including Soviet intervention against the 1956 Hungarian uprising.

key_facts.text: Khrushchev consolidated power after Stalin died in 1953.
His Secret Speech was delivered at the Soviet Communist Party's Twentieth Congress in February 1956.
The speech condemned Stalinist purges, including executions of party members.
Khrushchev advocated peaceful coexistence with the West.
He reached a secret missile-placement agreement with Fidel Castro in July 1962.

overview.text: Mark Antony, or Marcus Antonius, was a Roman general and politician closely allied with Julius Caesar. After Caesar's assassination in 44 BCE, Antony joined Caesar's adopted heir Octavian and Lepidus in the Second Triumvirate, a three-man governing alliance. Their forces defeated Caesar's assassins at Philippi in 42 BCE. Antony then became a leading power in Rome's eastern territories and formed a political and personal partnership with Cleopatra VII of Egypt. Rivalry with Octavian led to civil war. Octavian's forces defeated Antony and Cleopatra at the naval Battle of Actium in 31 BCE. Both died the following year, and Egypt came under Roman control.

overview.text: The Qin dynasty created the first centralized Chinese empire in 221 BCE, when its ruler Ying Zheng defeated the last rival Warring States and adopted the title Qin Shi Huang, or First Emperor. His government divided conquered territory into commanderies and standardized writing, currency, weights, and measures. It built roads and joined earlier northern defensive walls, an early stage in the history of the Great Wall. Qin rule also used harsh controls, including the burning of certain classical writings. The famous terracotta army guarded the emperor's tomb complex. Although the dynasty lasted only until 206 BCE, its model of centralized imperial administration influenced the Han dynasty that followed.

Qin rulers organized territory into commanderies under central authority.

Qin workers linked earlier northern walls; they did not build all of today's Great Wall.

overview.text: The Ming dynasty ruled China from 1368 to 1644, between the Yuan and Qing dynasties. Its early rulers rebuilt imperial authority after the Mongol-led Yuan period. The Yongle emperor moved the capital from Nanjing to Beijing and developed the palace complex later called the Forbidden City. Ming courts sponsored Zheng He's seven maritime expeditions between 1405 and 1433, reaching Southeast Asia, the Indian Ocean, and East Africa. The era is also known for accomplished porcelain, especially blue-and-white wares that circulated widely. Political and cultural activity continued long after the voyages ended; the dynasty's final crisis in the seventeenth century brought Qing rule to China.

overview.text: The “Blood and Iron” Speech was delivered by Prussian minister-president Otto von Bismarck to a parliamentary budget committee on September 30, 1862. Prussia's king wanted a larger army, while legislators disputed military spending and their budget powers. Bismarck argued that Prussia's strength, rather than liberal speeches or majority votes alone, would decide the major political questions facing the German states. He invoked the failed revolutions of 1848 and 1849 and favored a German nation-state dominated by Prussia. The surviving text is a reported summary in indirect speech, so its famous phrase should be treated as a recorded version rather than a perfectly certain word-for-word quotation.

overview.text: Francisco Pizarro was a Spanish conquistador who led the invasion that broke Inca imperial power in the 1530s. He entered the Andes while the empire was weakened by a succession war between Atahualpa and Huáscar and by disease. In November 1532, Pizarro's force captured Atahualpa at Cajamarca. The Inca ruler provided a vast ransom in precious metal, but Spanish captors executed him in 1533. Pizarro's men then advanced into the imperial heartland, relying in part on local allies and rivalries. He founded the Spanish city of Lima in 1535. The conquest brought colonial rule, dispossession, and lasting upheaval to Andean societies; resistance to Spain continued.

Atahualpa was executed in 1533 despite payment of a ransom.
The Inca succession war pitted Atahualpa against Huáscar.
Pizarro's invasion also benefited from local opponents of Inca rule.

overview.text: Troy was an ancient city in northwestern Anatolia, at the mound of Hisarlık near the Dardanelles in today's Turkey. Its ruins preserve a long sequence of fortified settlements, including a Bronze Age citadel and lower town. Later Greek and Roman inhabitants called the city Ilion or Ilium. Homer’s Iliad made Troy the setting of a war between Greeks and Trojans, giving the place an enormous literary afterlife. Excavations by Frank Calvert, Heinrich Schliemann, and later archaeologists exposed its many layers. The site is real, but scholars cannot identify a single excavated destruction with every event in the epic. UNESCO lists the archaeological site as World Heritage.

The mound contains multiple fortified Bronze Age settlement layers.

overview.text: Abolition of slavery is the legal ending of systems that treat people as property. It unfolded unevenly across countries and differed from ending the slave trade, which could leave enslaved people in bondage. British campaigners including Thomas Clarkson, Granville Sharp, and William Wilberforce pressed Parliament to end the trade in 1807; legislation passed in 1833 began abolition in much of the British Empire, with final emancipation after an apprenticeship period in 1838. The United States ratified the Thirteenth Amendment in 1865. In Brazil, Regent Princess Isabel signed the Golden Law in 1888, ending legal slavery there. Enslaved people's resistance and activism were central to these struggles, and legal freedom did not erase inequality.

key_facts.text: Britain abolished its transatlantic slave trade in 1807, before abolishing slavery in its colonies.
The 1833 British law was followed by an apprenticeship period ending in 1838.
The U.S. Thirteenth Amendment was ratified in 1865.

Brazil's law was signed by Regent Princess Isabel in the name of Emperor Pedro II.

overview.text: War is organized armed conflict involving states or other organized groups. It can take place between countries or within a country, where government forces and organized armed groups fight. Wars may arise from political, territorial, or other disputes, but the legal rules for armed conflict do not depend on either side formally declaring war. International humanitarian law, including the Geneva Conventions, sets limits on how fighting is conducted. It requires protection for civilians and humane treatment of people who are wounded, captured, or otherwise no longer fighting. The International Committee of the Red Cross distinguishes conflicts between states from conflicts involving organized armed groups inside a state.

key_facts.text: International armed conflict involves armed force between at least two states.
Non-international armed conflict can involve a state fighting an organized armed group.
A formal declaration of war is not required for humanitarian law to apply.

overview.text: Israel is a state on the eastern Mediterranean in the Levant, proclaimed on May 14, 1948, as Britain's mandate over Palestine ended. The United Nations had recommended dividing the mandate into Jewish and Arab states, with a special international arrangement for Jerusalem. The declaration was followed by war involving neighboring Arab states; the fighting also displaced many Palestinian Arabs, who fled or were expelled from areas that came under Israeli control. The war produced 1949 armistice lines rather than a comprehensive peace agreement. Israel joined the United Nations that year. Its history includes Jewish immigration and state-building alongside a continuing conflict over Palestinian refugees, territory, and security. These issues remain central to the region's history.
